items.license: CC BY 4.0 (stated on each paper page)
items.abstract: Quantum 10, 2275 (2026). https://doi.org/10.22331/q-2026-11-18-2275 We study the distinguishability of quantum states under local operations with classical communication (LOCC), separable, and positive-partial-transpose (PPT) measurements, focusing on locally diagonal orthogonally invariant (LDOI) states – those invariant under local diagonal orthogonal twirling. This class includes many important families such as Werner states, isotropic states, X-states, and Dicke states. We show that optimal PPT and separable measurements for distinguishing LDOI states can always be taken to be LDOI, and the LOCC supremum can be approached by LDOI LOCC POVMs, enabling a dimensional reduction from $n^4$ to $O(n^2)$ in the associated optimization problems. We establish efficiently computable bounds on the distinguishability of orthonormal LDOI bases and prove that for a broad class of such bases – including all two-qubit cases – the LOCC supremum equals the PPT and separable optima. More generally, we show the gap between PPT and LOCC distinguishability is at most $(n-2)/(2n^2)$ for local dimension $n$.

items.title: When should adaptation arise from a polygenic response versus few large-effect changes?
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by William R. Milligan, Laura K. Hayward, Guy Sella When will adaptation involve a few genetic changes of large effect versus a polygenic response? There are compelling reasons to expect polygenic adaptation to be common, yet direct evidence is lacking. Conversely, there are hundreds of examples of large-effect adaptations across species, but it is unclear whether they occur frequently within any given species. These different lines of evidence are hard to synthesize, in part due to the lack of theory that relates them. To address this gap, we frame the question in terms of the properties of an adaptive trait. We ask how the genetic basis of adaptation depends on key aspects of genetic variation in the trait and on the degree to which its selection pressures have changed. To this end, we consider a quantitative trait subject to stabilizing selection and model its response when a population at mutation–selection–drift balance experiences a sudden shift in the trait optimum. Using this model, we delimit how the contributions of large-effect and polygenic changes to adaptation depend on the genetics and ecology of adaptive traits, as well as on other salient factors. Thus, we formulate testable predictions for when different modes of adaptation are expected.

items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by Michael J. Stam, Diego A. Oyarzún, Nadanai Laohakunakorn, Christopher W. Wood Recent advancements in protein structure prediction methods have ushered in a new era of abundant and accurate structural data, providing opportunities to analyse proteins at a scale that has not been possible before. Here we performed a large-scale analysis of physicochemical properties across 373,779 confident AlphaFold structures. Our analysis revealed systematic variation between proteins from different organisms to such an extent that major features of the tree of life could be recovered from these data. items.title: Terminal shoot maturity orchestrates Carbon–Nitrogen balance and hormonal signaling to regulate floral induction in litchi (Litchi chinensis Sonn.)
items.license: CC BY 4.0 (verified on article pages; occasional CC0)
items.abstract: by Qiusheng Xiao, Yuqing Niu, Xingjie Li, Fayong Li Floral induction in litchi ( Litchi chinensis Sonn.) is triggered by chilling but strictly contingent upon terminal shoot maturity; however, the regulatory mechanism linking shoot status to floral fate remains elusive. This study investigated the physiological and molecular determinants of flowering in ‘Feizixiao’ litchi shoots of varying maturity under natural winter chilling. We found that shoot maturity is a prerequisite for flowering competency. Mature shoots accumulated significantly higher carbohydrate reserves (soluble sugars and starch), resulting in a high carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratio compared to immature shoots. Hormonal profiling revealed that maturation remodeled the hormonal landscape by upregulating abscisic acid (ABA) and suppressing gibberellin A 3 (GA 3 ). Expression analysis identified key flowering-regulatory genes, including promoters LcFT1 and LcSPL1 and repressors LcTFL1 and LcSPL6 . Correlation and PCA analyses identified the high ABA/GA 3 ratio and carbohydrate accumulation as intrinsic drivers activating the LcFT1 -mediated pathway. These findings suggest that shoot maturation coordinates a favorable metabolic and hormonal environment to unlock the genetic program for floral induction, providing a theoretical basis for managing alternate bearing in litchi.

items.abstract: Nucleolus is disassembled when the nuclear envelope breaks down during mitosis prophase. However, the dynamics of nucleolus in meiotic prophase remain unclear. Here, by tracking nucleolar components of spermatocytes in mice, we show that the nucleolus is fragmented even before the breakdown of the nuclear envelope. Instead of dissolving in nucleoplasm or cytoplasm, the nucleolar components are reaggregated and fused with the XY body during prophase I of meiosis. The dynamic relocation of the nucleolar components to the XY body is governed by the ATR-dependent signaling pathway. Moreover, the relocated pre-ribosomal RNA (pre-rRNA) covers the entire X and Y chromosomes. Surprisingly, this disruption of pre-rRNA induces the recruitment of RNA polymerase II to the XY body and partially abolishes meiotic sex chromosome inactivation (MSCI). items.abstract: Multidrug-resistant fungal pathogens are a serious threat to public health and global food security. Mitigation requires the discovery of antifungal compounds with novel modes of action along with a comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms governing antifungal resistance. Here, we apply saturated transposon analysis in yeast (SATAY), a powerful transposon sequencing method in Saccharomyces cerevisiae , to uncover loss- and gain-of-function mutations conferring resistance to 20 different antifungal compounds. These screens identify a diverse array of novel resistance mechanisms and multiple modes of action. SATAY is performed in drug-sensitive strains to generate chemogenomic profiles for compounds that lack activity against conventional laboratory strains. This study therefore provides a significant resource for exploring cellular responses to chemical stresses. We discover that the natural antifungal chitosan electrostatically interacts with cell wall mannosylphosphate and that the transporter Hol1 concentrates the novel antifungal ATI-2307 within yeast. This latter finding presents an avenue for drug design initiatives but also unveils a straightforward evolutionary path to ATI-2307 resistance with minimal fitness cost.

items.title: Motivo: A Motif-Based Algorithm-Architecture Co-Design for Fast and Energy-Efficient Graph-Based Genome Analysis
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Read mapping, a key step of genome sequence analysis, matches each fragment of a sequenced genome (a read) to its location in a reference genome. A genome graph is a graph-based reference genome that represents the genetic diversity of a population as alternative paths, and thus improves read mapping accuracy. However, the size and complexity of a genome graph make sequence-to-graph (S2G) mapping a major bottleneck. Prior software and hardware approaches for S2G mapping perform redundant costly operations (e.g., graph traversals and dynamic programming) that do not lead to valid mappings. Our key observation is that a genome graph consists of small subgraphs that share a limited set of recurring topologies, which we call motifs. We propose Motivo, a topology-aware algorithm-architecture co-design for S2G mapping. Motivo's algorithm uses motifs in two ways. First, it stores the precomputed motifs of each node in a compact index, which replaces a graph traversal with a single memory lookup. Second, it uses the topology of a motif and the properties of its nodes to identify the few most suitable mapping paths with arithmetic operations. The algorithm enables high-performance execution on CPUs and GPUs and high-performance, low-energy execution on Motivo-ASIC, an accelerator we co-design with it. Motivo-CPU provides 2.1-18.4x, 2.8-343x, and 1.4-10.1x speedups over GraphAligner, vg, and minigraph, and Motivo-GPU provides 1.5-1.6x speedups over vg-giraffe. Motivo-ASIC provides 7.4-11.7x (138-274x) speedups over state-of-the-art CPU-based tools for short (long) reads. Compared to SeGraM (short reads) and HARP (long reads), Motivo-ASIC achieves 5.3x and 4.0-4.3x higher throughput per Watt and 1.7x and 2.7-3.0x higher throughput per mm$^2$, respectively. Motivo maintains equal or higher mapping accuracy than other tools (96.8%-99.7%) for short and long reads on two types of genome graphs.

items.title: FastCREST: GPU-Accelerated CREST Conformer Searches with Consistent Energies and Gradients
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: CREST conformer searches with GFN2-xTB take days for large, flexible molecules: one search of a 274-atom gallium(III)--peptide complex with CREST 3.0.2 took 321.5~h on 32 CPU threads. FastCREST keeps CREST's algorithm and changes how a search uses the hardware. Its metadynamics (MTD) and molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories run with tuned OpenMP settings and one GPU, which solves the self-consistent-charge (SCC) eigenproblem and evaluates the three-body dispersion term. About 15,000 geometry optimizations per iteration run as Slurm array jobs on other CPU nodes, and checkpoints let a search continue on preemptible GPUs. On A100 nodes, the OpenMP settings and loop changes made an MTD step 2.4 times faster and the GPU another 2.3 times; array jobs made a batch of optimizations 39 times faster. For six more molecules of 24 to 339 atoms, a FastCREST step was 2.2 to 7.1 times faster than a conventional CREST step. A complete FastCREST search, which also lifts CREST~3's cap of 200 optimization cycles, took 54.3~h, evaluating energies and gradients 8.1 times as fast as the CREST 3.0.2 search (on different hardware) with fewer CPU-hours per evaluation. Two opt-in settings (a warm-started Jacobi eigensolver and GPU-resident SCC iterations), LLVM's OpenMP library and one CPU socket per trajectory made an MTD step 8.3 times faster than conventional CREST. Energies agree with CREST 3.0.2 within $1.01\times10^{-10}$ Eh and gradients within $8.2\times10^{-11}$Eh bohr$^{-1}$, and controlled MD runs passed a prespecified equivalence test. Most replicate FastCREST and conventional CREST searches ended in similar compact conformers, with no detectable difference in energy.

items.title: A kinetic error filtering mechanism for enzyme-free copying of nucleic acid sequences
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Accurate copying of nucleic acid sequences is essential for self-replicating systems. Modern cells achieve error ratios as low as 10−9 with sophisticated enzymes capable of kinetic proofreading. In contrast, experiments probing enzyme-free copying of RNA and DNA as potential prebiotic replication processes find error ratios on the order of 10%. Given this low intrinsic copying fidelity, plausible scenarios for the spontaneous emergence of molecular evolution require an accuracy-enhancing mechanism. Here, we study a 'kinetic error filtering' scenario that dramatically boosts the likelihood of producing exact copies of nucleic acid sequences. The mechanism exploits the observation that initial errors in template-directed polymerization of both DNA and RNA are likely to trigger a cascade of consecutive errors and significantly stall downstream extension. We incorporate these characteristics into a mathematical model with experimentally estimated parameters, and leverage this model to probe to what extent accurate and faulty polymerization products can be kinetically discriminated. items.title: Blood-derived dietary protein promotes sleep in the mosquito Aedes aegypti
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Sleep is a ubiquitous, yet highly variable, behavior across species. The duration and timing of sleep are influenced by ecological demands and dietary context. In the mosquito Aedes aegypti , a blood-feeding insect with specialized nutritional requirements, the relationship between feeding and sleep remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how blood-derived dietary protein influences sleep regulation. Using postural analysis, videography, and arousal-threshold assays, we established that immobility bouts of ≥10 min reliably define sleep in A. aegypti . Mosquitoes lacking the circadian clock gene cycle still maintained daily sleep rhythms but exhibited reduced sleep duration and heightened overall activity. Infrared activity monitoring revealed that blood-fed females showed a marked increase in sleep beginning immediately after feeding and persisting for several days, accompanied by reduced locomotor activity. Notably, this sleep elevation lasted well beyond the cessation of previously reported host-seeking phases, raising the possibility of distinct phases of opportunistic vs. targeted host pursuit. To determine the dietary basis of this effect, we tested mosquitoes fed a bovine serum albumin (BSA)-based diet. BSA feeding alone was sufficient to mimic the sleep-promoting and activity-reducing effects of blood, suggesting dietary protein is a major nutritional regulator.

Using a newly developed 2D fiber-retraction assay, we observed a ‘gearwheel’ pattern of actomyosin in spread platelets with associated, extracellular fibrin patches that appear to initiate fibrin fiber attachment and rearrangement. The outcome of this process results in two morphologically different platelet populations. Spread platelets with coiled fibers around and above their pseudo-nucleus. Other, only partially spread platelets have tightly packed fibers around bulbous protrusions (‘bulbs’), mirroring the architecture of platelets and adjacent fibers within a retracted clot. Thus, the observed compaction process might take place during clot retraction to reduce clot volume, stiffen the clot, and enhance wound repair. Apart from pulling on fibers like on a rope, platelets actively wrap them into compact structures, similar to balls of wool. items.title: Diurnal rhythmicity in metabolism and salivary effector expression shapes aphid performance on host plants
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Diurnal rhythms influence insect behavior, physiology, and metabolism, optimizing their performance by adapting to daily changes in the environment. While their impact on agricultural pests has been briefly explored, our understanding of how these rhythms drive adaptive responses in pest biology and influence host colonization remains elusive. Here, we show that a notorious global aphid pest, Rhopalosiphum padi , exhibits distinct diurnal patterns in feeding behavior, with elevated honeydew excretion at night and extended phloem salivation during early nighttime. Temporal aphid transcriptome profiling reveals four diurnally rhythmic clusters, two of which peak at night, exhibiting enrichment in carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism. Beyond the established role in manipulating host responses and allowing sustained feeding, our study reveals novel evidence of cyclical fluctuations in salivary effector expression in an insect species. Silencing key effector genes, peaking in expression during the increased nighttime salivation, results in a more pronounced reduction in aphid excretion activity on host plants during the night compared to the day, a phenomenon not observed on artificial diets. items.title: GEI-17-mediated SUMOylation of GDP dissociation inhibitor GDI-1 regulates apoptotic cell clearance
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by Lei Yuan, Peiyao Li, Aiying Ma, Chao Li, Fuqiao Liu, Yunmin Xie, Qian Zheng, Hui Wang, Hui Xiao Apoptotic cell clearance represents the final stage of apoptosis and involves phagosome formation, maturation, and digestion. Here, we found that SUMO modifications participate in apoptotic cell clearance by influencing phagosomal degradation activity in C. elegans . The SUMO E3 ligase, GEI-17, SUMOylates GDP dissociation inhibitor (GDI-1) at K270 to trigger phagosomal degradation. Upon SUMOylation, GDI-1 facilitates release of GDP-bound RAB-1, which is subsequently converted to the GTP-bound form in a manner dependent on GDI displacement factor, PRAF-3. RAB-1 conversion enables binding and translocation of RAB-7 from the endoplasmic reticulum to Golgi to promote phagosome maturation and degradation activity. In the absence of GDI-1 SUMOylation, GDI-1 binds to GDP-RAB-1, sequestering it in the cytoplasm, resulting in impaired phagosomal degradation. Furthermore, we found SUMOylation of GDI1 at a conserved site plays a crucial role in efferocytosis regulation in mammals. This study defines a previously unrecognized mechanism by which SUMOylation drives apoptotic cell clearance.

items.title: Ionic condition-dependent allostery shapes ribosomal dynamics
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by Danis Yangaliev, Gürol M. Süel, S. Banu Ozkan Ionic composition is a key determinant of ribosomal RNA structure and function. Metal cations such as potassium (K + ) and magnesium (Mg 2+ ) stabilize rRNA architecture. While certain positions in the ribosome are strictly occupied by either potassium or magnesium for distinct structural or functional reasons, their broader role in modulating ribosomal dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we use microsecond-scale coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of the bacterial 70S ribosome to examine how ionic composition affects structural flexibility and long-range communication. We compare a native ribosome with experimentally resolved ions to two variants: a magnesium-enriched model, in which K + ions are replaced with Mg 2+ , and a hydrated magnesium model. While these substitutions do not aim to reproduce physiological ionic conditions, they provide a controlled framework to isolate the physical effects of ion identity on ribosomal dynamics. Increasing magnesium content reduces ionic and backbone mobility and enhances rigidity within the ribosomal core. Dynamic Flexibility Index analysis shows that these changes extend beyond local coordination sites, producing flexibility shifts at distances exceeding 30 Å. Dynamic Coupling Index analysis further reveals that ionic perturbations reshape long-range communication pathway

items.title: Symmetries, correlation functions, and entanglement of general quantum Motzkin spin-chains
items.license: CC BY 4.0 (stated on each paper page)
items.abstract: Quantum 10, 2279 (2026). https://doi.org/10.22331/q-2026-11-20-2279 Motzkin spin-chains, which include `colorless' (integer spin $s=1$) and `colorful' ($s \geq 2$) variants, are one-dimensional (1D) local integer spin models notable for their lack of a conformal field theory (CFT) description of their low-energy physics, despite being gapless. The colorful variants are particularly unusual, as they exhibit power-law violation of the area-law of entanglement entropy (as $\sqrt{n}$ in system size $n$), rather than a logarithmic violation as seen in a CFT. In this work, we analytically discover several unique properties of these models, potentially suggesting a new universality class for their low-energy physics. We identify a complex structure of symmetries and unexpected scaling behavior in spin-spin correlations, which deviate from known 1D universality classes. Specifically, the $s=1$ chain exhibits $U(1)$ spontaneous symmetry breaking and ferromagnetic order. Meanwhile, the $s \geq 2$ chains do not appear to spontaneously break any symmetries, but display quasi-long-range algebraic order with power-law decaying correlations, inconsistent with standard Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) critical exponents. items.title: Improved parameter initialization for the (local) unitary cluster Jastrow ansatz
items.license: CC BY 4.0 (stated on each paper page)
items.abstract: Quantum 10, 2278 (2026). https://doi.org/10.22331/q-2026-11-19-2278 The unitary cluster Jastrow (UCJ) ansatz and its variant known as local UCJ (LUCJ) are promising choices for variational quantum algorithms for chemistry due to their combination of physical motivation and hardware efficiency. The parameters of these ansatzes can be initialized from the output of a coupled cluster, singles and doubles (CCSD) calculation performed on a classical computer. However, truncating the number of repetitions of the ansatz, as well as discarding interactions to accommodate the connectivity constraints of near-term quantum processors, degrade the approximation to CCSD and the resulting energy accuracy. In this work, we propose two methods to improve the parameter initialization. The first method, which is applicable to both expectation value- and sample-based algorithms, uses compressed double factorization of the CCSD amplitudes to improve or recover the CCSD approximation. The second method, which is applicable to sample-based algorithms, uses approximate tensor network simulation to improve the quality of samples produced by the ansatz circuit. Both methods perform classical preprocessing to construct the initial circuit parameters and can be followed by parameter optimization using quantum measurements, although we do not perform such optimization in this work.
